reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: Ohtani is the most complete baseball player on the planet, and the Statcast profile makes that impossible to argue — his bat registers an xwOBA of .412 and xSLG of .563 with a 93.6 mph average exit velocity, all sitting in the 96th-to-98th percentile range, while his 15.2% walk rate checks in near the top of the league and his barrel rate of 16.4% is elite. On the mound, the xERA of 2.68 and xwOBA against of .257 are both 94th percentile stuff, backed by a 98.0 mph fastball with 2485 rpm of spin and a 30.9% whiff rate — he's a legitimate front-of-rotation arm, not a novelty act. The one real tension in his profile is contact quality allowed: his 7.7% walk rate as a pitcher is workable but not dominant, and his K% as a hitter (23.0%) shows he's not untouchable from the other side of the ball either. ValuCast projects a .283/.397/.547 slash with 39 homers over 699 PA — the medium confidence tag is almost entirely about workload and health for a two-way player at 31, not any doubt about the skill.

His average exit velocity of 92.4 mph and 14.1% barrel rate put him in the top tier of contact quality in the league, and a 28.8 ft/s sprint speed gives him real stolen-base upside on top of the thump. The one thing standing between him and a true star line is the chase — 32.6% puts him well below average in zone discipline, which is why the xBA (.255) lags behind the xSLG (.475) and why ValuCast's projection lands at .279/.336/.494 with 26 home runs rather than something scarier. If the approach tightens even modestly, the power-speed combination here becomes hard to ignore; if it doesn't, he's a volatile middle-of-the-order bat who'll beat you some nights and give away at-bats on others.

reports.name: Pete Alonso
reports.published_report: Pete Alonso is one of the purest power hitters in the game right now, and the Statcast profile backs that up without apology — 94.1 mph average exit velocity and a 53.8% hard-hit rate both sit in the 97th percentile, and his .515 xSLG tells you the raw thump is real, not context-dependent. The thing that keeps him from being a true MVP-tier bat is the strikeout side: a 27.8% whiff rate and 24.7% K% both sit below the 33rd percentile, meaning pitchers with quality stuff can carve him up, and his .248 projected AVG reflects that friction directly. ValuCast's projection of 35 HR and a .812 OPS over 686 PA is a clean, bankable outcome for a middle-of-the-order corner bat — not a surprise upside play, just a guy who hits the ball as hard as almost anyone alive and does enough else to cash it.

reports.name: Aaron Judge
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power disconnect is the whole story with Judge right now: his xSLG sits at .600 (99th percentile) and his barrel rate is 21.7% (100th percentile), but a 32.2% whiff rate (12th percentile) is keeping that elite raw power from fully translating — hence the xBA of .270 at just the 75th percentile. The walk rate at 16.1% (98th percentile) keeps him dangerous even when pitchers attack him, and the underlying quality of contact is as good as anyone in the sport. ValuCast's projection of .257/.387/.545 with 27 home runs in 411 PA reflects that tension: the power is real and historic, but the strikeouts are a real tax, and at 33 with sprint speed in the 33rd percentile, this is a player whose value now lives almost entirely in the batter's box.

reports.name: Cody Bellinger
reports.published_report: Bellinger is a plate-discipline hitter who earns his numbers through contact quality and zone management, not raw thump — and his Statcast card makes that split explicit. His BB% (13.6%, 90th percentile) and K% (14.1%, 86th percentile) are genuinely elite, and the 19.0% whiff rate (81st percentile) backs up a real ability to make consistent contact, which is why xBA sits at .281 (86th percentile) even though his exit velocity (89.0 mph, 44th percentile) and Hard-Hit% (36.9%, 30th percentile) are ordinary at best. The power projection — 23 HR, .441 SLG in 671 PA — depends on him continuing to put the ball in the air enough to let ordinary contact play, because he's not going to carry a slugging line on authority alone. The walk rate and strikeout suppression are the load-bearing skills here; as long as those hold, the .257/.344/.441 projection (ValuCast, current) is real.

reports.published_report: Henry Bolte is a 22-year-old center fielder doing something rare at Triple-A: hitting for average and power at the same time, with the stolen bases to make the whole profile breathe. His .348/.418/.658 line in 177 PA this season comes with a .310 ISO and 17 steals — the MLB-equivalent translation puts his ISO at .196 against a league average of .150, and his K% (22.8%) essentially mirrors the majors' norm, so the bat isn't just inflated by the level. The one real question is approach — a 10% walk rate looks fine on the surface, but the projection has him at a 45 on BB%, and the gap between his power ceiling and his discipline suggests the games where the swing gets long could cost him at the next level. reports.name: Leo De Vries
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 306 PA.
reports.published_report: Leo De Vries is a 19-year-old shortstop doing something genuinely rare at AA: hitting for average, working counts, and stealing bases at a volume that makes him a different kind of threat than the raw power types ahead of him in most systems. His .279/.372/.420 line (AA, 306 PA) comes with 28 steals, an 11% walk rate, and a 21% strikeout rate — that contact-and-patience combination is what earns him a 78th-percentile average mark and a 71st-percentile OBP against his minor-league peer group. The honest limiting factor is power: nine home runs and a .141 ISO translate to roughly .124 at the MLB level, well below the .150 average, and that gap is what caps the ceiling. The projection sees a low-end everyday regular as the upside with a floor of bench depth, and ValuCast has him cooling — down 3.3 score points over the last three days — which tracks with the profile being speed-and-contact dependent in a way that leaves him without a true carrying tool if the hit rate softens.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report: Oneil Cruz is one of the most violent contact-makers in baseball — 96.0 mph average exit velocity and 59.2% hard-hit rate both sit at the 100th percentile — but he gives a huge chunk of it back at the plate because he simply can't make consistent contact, whiffing at 37.8% (2nd percentile) with a 34.6% K% that ranks dead last. The .358 xwOBA (81st percentile) and .490 xSLG (86th percentile) tell you the raw damage is real when he connects, and the ValuCast projection of 23 HR and 33 SB in 497 PA reflects a player who can hurt you in multiple ways. The strikeout rate is the whole story — if it doesn't come down, he'll always be a boom-or-bust guy who leaves production on the table, and the 10.6% BB% suggests the zone awareness is there enough to keep him from being unplayable. Medium confidence here is honest: the power and speed are elite, the bat-to-ball is a genuine problem, and the gap between those two facts is what Cruz's career hinges on.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 36.7 IP.

His 15.0 K/9 at A+ sits in the 98th percentile among arms in this pool — the swing-and-miss is real. The problem is the 8.1 BB/9, which translates to a 6.0 BB/9 MLB equivalent against a league average of 3.2, and that's what's driving the 6.10 ERA and 1.90 WHIP. The K-BB% lands at 16%, which is functional on paper, but the walk total is eating every margin he creates with the strikeout. reports.name: Bryson Stott
reports.published_report: Stott is a speed-and-contact second baseman whose value lives almost entirely in his legs and his ability to put the ball in play — not in doing damage when he does. The Statcast profile confirms it: 17.4% whiff rate and a 72nd-percentile xBA (.264) say he makes consistent contact, but 89.1 mph average exit velocity, a 6.9% barrel rate, and a 38th-percentile hard-hit rate say he's not hurting anyone when he squares one up. The projection — .248/.314/.391 with 13 home runs and 28 steals across 584 PA — is essentially what the Statcast card predicts: a guy whose OBP undersells his contact quality because his 7.4% walk rate won't carry water, and whose stolen-base total is the one number that keeps him roster-relevant in mixed formats. The 33.0% chase rate (30th percentile) is the quiet concern; if pitchers learn to expand his zone, that xBA advantage shrinks fast.
